summary: The priestly offering rules conclude with the trespass offering, priestly shares, and three occasions for peace offerings: thanksgiving, a vow, or a freewill gift. The chapter regulates when sacrificial meat may be eaten, excludes people or meat in an unclean state, reserves blood and designated fat, and assigns the breast and right thigh to the priests.
whyItMatters: This chapter completes the offering collection by showing how altar portions, priestly portions, and permitted meals fit together under boundaries of time, purity, and assigned ownership.

context.author: The chapter continues ritual instructions presented as Yahweh's commands through Moses; it does not identify the book's narrator or final compiler.
context.audience: Priests who perform the offerings and Israelites who bring and eat from peace offerings.
context.date: The narrative setting is Israel's time at Sinai; the chapter itself does not date its composition.
context.setting: At the altar and in holy eating places near the Tent of Meeting, with some rules extending to Israel's dwellings.
context.literaryForm: Supplementary ritual law completing the instructions for the major offerings introduced in chapters 1-6.

outline.heading: Trespass offering and priestly portions
outline.note: The chapter details the altar portions and distributes meat, hides, and grain preparations among priests.

outline.heading: A peace offering for thanksgiving
outline.note: Several breads accompany the sacrifice, and its meat must be eaten on the day it is offered.

outline.heading: Vow and freewill peace offerings
outline.note: These may be eaten through the next day, but third-day meat must be burned.

outline.heading: Purity boundaries for the meal
outline.note: Unclean meat is burned, and an unclean person may not eat meat belonging to Yahweh.

outline.heading: Fat and blood reserved from eating
outline.note: The law distinguishes other uses for some fat but prohibits eating sacrificial fat or any blood.

outline.heading: Breast and thigh assigned to the priests
outline.note: The worshiper brings the offering by hand, the fat is burned, and designated portions support Aaron's house.

outline.heading: Summary of the offering laws
outline.note: The closing list locates the full collection in Yahweh's command to Moses at Sinai.

keyVerses.text: The flesh of the sacrifice of his peace offerings for thanksgiving shall be eaten on the day of his offering. He shall not leave any of it until the morning.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the strict time limit for the thanksgiving meal, which differs from the next case.

keyVerses.text: If any of the meat of the sacrifice of his peace offerings is eaten on the third day, it will not be accepted, and it shall not be credited to him who offers it. It will be an abomination, and the soul who eats any of it will bear his iniquity.
keyVerses.why: The third-day warning makes the meal's timing part of whether the offering is accepted.

keyVerses.text: You shall not eat any blood, whether it is of bird or of animal, in any of your dwellings.
keyVerses.why: The prohibition on consuming blood applies to birds and animals in any dwelling, not just at the sanctuary.

keyVerses.text: For the waved breast and the heaved thigh I have taken from the children of Israel out of the sacrifices of their peace offerings, and have given them to Aaron the priest and to his sons as their portion forever from the children of Israel.’”
keyVerses.why: The verse identifies the breast and thigh as a lasting assigned portion rather than an informal payment.

questions.question: How is the trespass offering handled?
questions.answer: It is killed where the burnt offering is killed, its blood is sprinkled around the altar, and the listed fat and organs are burned. The priests may eat the remaining holy meat in a holy place, following the same basic law as the sin offering.

questions.question: Which priest receives which part of an offering?
questions.answer: The officiating priest receives a burnt offering’s skin and baked or cooked meal offerings. The sin and trespass offerings are assigned to priestly use, and verse 6 says every male among the priests may eat the latter in a holy place. Meal offerings mixed with oil or left dry are shared among all Aaron’s sons.

questions.question: What do thanksgiving, vow, and freewill mean in the peace-offering rules?
questions.answer: They name three occasions for bringing a peace offering. Thanksgiving receives its own bread and same-day eating rule, while an offering connected with a vow or freely chosen gift may also be eaten on the following day.

questions.question: Why does a thanksgiving offering include leavened bread?
questions.answer: Verse 13 explicitly includes leavened bread alongside the unleavened cakes and wafers, and verse 14 assigns one of each as a priestly contribution. The chapter does not explain why this accompanying bread differs from grain burned on the altar.

questions.question: Are the one-day and two-day limits ancient food-safety advice?
questions.answer: The text treats them as ritual boundaries tied to the offering's acceptance: thanksgiving meat is eaten the same day, while vow or freewill meat may extend one day longer. It gives no medical rationale, and third-day meat is condemned in sacrificial terms rather than explained scientifically.

questions.question: Does ritual uncleanness in verses 19-21 mean moral sin?
questions.answer: No. The passage distinguishes meat that contacted an unclean thing from a person who is in an unclean state and therefore may not eat holy meat. These are ritual access rules; the chapter does not call the affected person dirty, wicked, or less valuable.

questions.question: What does “cut off from his people” mean?
questions.answer: The phrase marks a severe consequence for eating holy meat while unclean or for consuming prohibited fat or blood. The chapter does not describe a human enforcement procedure or specify exactly how this loss of standing among the people occurs.

questions.question: Does the rule about fat and blood make a modern health claim?
questions.answer: No such rationale appears. The passage reserves the fat of animals offered by fire and prohibits consuming blood in any dwelling; it even permits nonfood uses for fat from an animal that died or was torn, showing that the rule is specifically about eating.

questions.question: What are the waved breast and heaved thigh?
questions.answer: They are portions of a peace offering presented before Yahweh and then assigned to Aaron and his sons. The worshiper brings the fat and breast by hand, the priest burns the fat, and the named breast and thigh become the priests' continuing share.

glossary.def: A peace offering brought in thanks, accompanied here by several breads and eaten on the day it is offered.
A peace offering connected with a formal promise, with meat permitted through the following day.
A portion presented before Yahweh and then assigned for priestly use, represented here by the breast.
A severe covenantal penalty whose exact mechanism is not defined within this chapter.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: Chapter 6 moves from repairing property wrongdoing to the priests’ management of the altar fire and their portions of meal and sin offerings.

here.text: The offering instructions conclude with trespass and peace-offering procedures, priestly shares, meal timing, purity restrictions, and the prohibition on eating designated fat or blood.

after.text: The next chapter enacts these instructions in the public consecration of Aaron and his sons, performed by Moses before the congregation.
